 Lawmakers press USDA for details on how food assistance cuts are affecting older adults
 By Krystal Knapp 
 Oct 27, 2026 Oct 27, 2026 
 Email Subscribe WhatsApp SMS Share 
 Expanded work requirements and the proposed elimination of federal senior nutrition program raise concerns about hunger among older Americans. 
 New Jersey’s food assistance rolls have shrunk by more than 71,000 people in the past year, and a proposal to eliminate a federal nutrition program for seniors could put thousands of additional residents at risk of going hungry.
 U.S. Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-11th District, and 17 other Democratic lawmakers are demanding that the Trump administration explain how changes to federal nutrition programs are affecting older Americans and what steps the government is taking to protect them from going hungry
 In an Oct. 27 letter to Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins , the lawmakers raised concerns about expanded work requirements for food assistance and the administration’s proposal to eliminate a separate nutrition program serving nearly 700,000 low-income seniors nationwide.
 The letter comes as New Jersey is already experiencing a significant decline in participation in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps.
 The number of state residents receiving SNAP benefits fell by approximately 71,300 between June 2025 and June 2026, from 810,900 to 739,600, according to an October report from the New Jersey Department of Human Services . Department officials estimate the law will ultimately reduce SNAP enrollment by about 49,500 people per average month.
 The federal spending and tax law signed by President Donald Trump in July 2025 is projected to reduce federal SNAP spending by approximately $187 billion through 2034, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
 Among other changes, the law expanded work requirements to adults ages 55 through 64 who previously were exempt based on age. Those subject to the requirements must document at least 80 hours of work or qualifying activities each month or risk losing benefits after three months.
 The lawmakers warned that older adults may have difficulty meeting those requirements because of health problems and barriers to employment. They cited research finding that more than half of low-income adults ages 55 to 64 who would be subject to the expanded requirements reported a health-related barrier to working.
 Meanwhile, the Trump administration’s proposed federal budget for fiscal year 2027 calls for eliminating the Commodity Supplemental Food Program, which provides monthly packages of nutritious food to nearly 700,000 low-income adults ages 60 and older nationwide.
 In New Jersey, the program serves about 4,865 low-income seniors each month, according to the state’s September 2026 operating plan .
 The administration has proposed shifting its focus to SNAP to support seniors, but lawmakers questioned that approach given the new restrictions on SNAP eligibility and benefits. Congress has maintained funding for the supplemental food program despite previous proposals to eliminate it.
 Lawmakers are asking the U.S. Department of Agriculture to provide state-by-state data showing how many adults ages 55 to 64 have lost SNAP benefits, had their assistance reduced, or received exemptions from the new work requirements. They also want information about the potential health and financial consequences of eliminating the supplemental food program, along with the administration’s plans to maintain access to nutritious food. Their letter requests a written response by Nov. 6.
 “Older Americans who spent their lives working and contributing to their communities should not have to sacrifice their health, housing, or other basic needs just to put food on the table,” the lawmakers wrote. “Your Department must account for the consequences of these policies and demonstrate how it will protect older Americans from hunger.”
 Mejia led a coalition of 17 other Democratic representatives in sending a letter to U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins. The letter was also signed by Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois, Frederica Wilson of Florida, Jasmine Crockett of Texas, Cleo Fields of Louisiana, André Carson of Indiana, Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, Nanette Diaz Barragán of California, Debbie Wasserman Schultz of Florida, Robert Garcia of California, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Eleanor Holmes Norton of Washington, D.C., Sylvia Garcia of Texas, Pramila Jayapal of Washington, Paul Tonko of New York, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Jesús “Chuy” García of Illinois, and Andrea Salinas of Oregon.
